title: Πίθηκος καὶ δελφίς
part: The Monkey and the Dolphin (Chambry 305 · Perry 73)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 305 (= Perry 73). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔθους ὄντος τοῖς πλέουσι Μελιταῖα κυνίδια καὶ πιθήκους ἐπάγεσθαι πρὸς παραμυθίαν τοῦ πλοῦ, πλέων τις εἶχε σὺν ἑαυτῷ καὶ πίθηκον.
sentences.tr: Ethous ontos tois pleousi Melitaia kynidia kai pithēkous epagesthai pros paramythian tou plou, pleōn tis eiche syn heautōi kai pithēkon.
sentences.l: It being the custom for those who sail to bring along Maltese lap-dogs and monkeys for the easing of the voyage, a certain man on a voyage had a monkey with him too.
sentences.i: It was the custom for seafarers to take Maltese lap-dogs and monkeys aboard to relieve the tedium of the voyage, and so a man making a voyage had a monkey with him as well.
sentences.n: The fable opens with a genitive absolute (Ἔθους ὄντος) setting the standing custom before the particular voyage — the regular scene-setting move in this collection. Μελιταῖα κυνίδια are the small Maltese dogs kept as pets in antiquity, the diminutive κυνίδιον marking their size. παραμυθία is the easing of a thing that would otherwise be hard to bear.

sentences.t: Γενομένων δ’ αὐτῶν κατὰ τὸ Σούνιον, τὸ τῆς Ἀττικῆς ἀκρωτήριον, χειμῶνα σφοδρὸν συνέβη γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr: Genomenōn d’ autōn kata to Sounion, to tēs Attikēs akrōtērion, cheimōna sphodron synebē genesthai.
sentences.l: And they having come to be off Sunium, the headland of Attica, it happened that a violent storm arose.
sentences.i: When they were off Sunium, the headland of Attica, a violent storm came on.
sentences.n: χειμών is 'winter' and so 'storm'; here plainly the second. κατά + acc. of place is 'down at, off' — the position of a ship abreast of a landmark. Sunium is the southern cape of Attica, the point a ship rounds coming up the coast to Athens, so the wreck happens within sight of home.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ νεὼς περιτραπείσης καὶ πάντων διακολυμβώντων, ἐνήχετο καὶ ὁ πίθηκος.
sentences.tr: Tēs de neōs peritrapeisēs kai pantōn diakolymbōntōn, enēcheto kai ho pithēkos.
sentences.l: And the ship having been overturned and all swimming across, the monkey too was swimming.
sentences.i: The ship capsized, and while all of them were swimming for it, the monkey too was swimming.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes again, sharing one δέ. καί before ὁ πίθηκος is 'too', not 'and' — it puts the monkey among the swimmers and so sets up the mistake that follows.

sentences.t: Δελφὶς δέ τις αὐτὸν θεασάμενος καὶ ἄνθρωπον εἶναι ὑπολαβών, ὑπελθὼν ἀνεῖχε διακομίζων ἐπὶ τὴν χέρσον.
sentences.tr: Delphis de tis auton theasamenos kai anthrōpon einai hypolabōn, hypelthōn aneiche diakomizōn epi tēn cherson.
sentences.l: And a certain dolphin, having caught sight of him and having supposed him to be a man, having gone in under him, held him up, carrying him across to the dry land.
sentences.i: A dolphin caught sight of him and took him for a man, and going in underneath him held him up and carried him toward the shore.
sentences.n: The chain of aorist participles running into a single main verb is the engine of these fables: three prior actions, then ἀνεῖχε in the imperfect for the one that goes on. ὑπολαμβάνω here is 'take up, and so suppose' — a verb of thinking, with accusative and infinitive after it. Dolphins rescuing men from the sea are a fixed piece of Greek lore, not a joke of this fable's own.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ κατὰ τὸν Πειραιᾶ ἐγένετο, τὸ τῶν Ἀθηναίων ἐπίνειον, ἐπυνθάνετο τοῦ πιθήκου εἰ τὸ γένος ἐστὶν Ἀθηναῖος.
sentences.tr: Hōs de kata ton Peiraia egeneto, to tōn Athēnaiōn epineion, epynthaneto tou pithēkou ei to genos estin Athēnaios.
sentences.l: And when he came off Piraeus, the port of the Athenians, he inquired of the monkey whether he was an Athenian by race.
sentences.n: πυνθάνομαι takes the genitive of the person asked (τοῦ πιθήκου). τὸ γένος is an accusative of respect, 'in respect of birth'. An ἐπίνειον is the harbour town belonging to an inland city, as Piraeus belongs to Athens — the word matters, because the dolphin's next question turns on Piraeus being a place.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ εἰπόντος καὶ λαμπρῶν ἐνταῦθα τετυχηκέναι γονέων, ἐπανήρετο εἰ καὶ τὸν Πειραιᾶ ἐπίσταται.
sentences.tr: Tou de eipontos kai lamprōn entautha tetychēkenai goneōn, epanēreto ei kai ton Peiraia epistatai.
sentences.l: And he having said so, and that he had got illustrious parents there, the dolphin asked further whether he knew Piraeus as well.
sentences.i: The monkey said that he was, and that he came of distinguished parents there, and the dolphin asked further whether he knew Piraeus too.
sentences.n: τυγχάνω with the genitive is 'obtain, get', and of parents it is the Greek for coming of a certain stock. The perfect infinitive τετυχηκέναι reports the monkey's own perfect. ἐπανέρομαι is to put a further question on top of the first.

sentences.t: Ὑπολαβὼν δὲ ὁ πίθηκος περὶ ἀνθρώπου αὐτὸν λέγειν, ἔφη καὶ μάλα φίλον εἶναι αὐτῷ καὶ συνήθη.
sentences.tr: Hypolabōn de ho pithēkos peri anthrōpou auton legein, ephē kai mala philon einai autōi kai synēthē.
sentences.l: And the monkey, having supposed that he was speaking about a man, said that he was indeed a very great friend to him and an intimate.
sentences.i: The monkey supposed that he was speaking of a man, and said that Piraeus was a great friend of his and an old acquaintance.
sentences.n: The fable's hinge: the monkey hears a harbour's name as a person's. καὶ μάλα is an intensifier, 'and very much so'. συνήθης is one you are used to, a familiar — the same word as the συνήθεια, 'habit', of other morals.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ δελφὶς ἐπὶ τοσούτῳ ψεύδει ἀγανακτήσας, βαπτίζων αὐτὸν ἀπέκτεινεν.
sentences.tr: Kai ho delphis epi tosoutōi pseudei aganaktēsas, baptizōn auton apekteinen.
sentences.l: And the dolphin, having grown indignant at so great a lie, dipping him under, killed him.
sentences.i: And the dolphin, indignant at so great a lie, pushed him under and drowned him.
sentences.n: ἐπί + dat. gives the ground of an emotion, 'indignant at'. βαπτίζω is to dip a thing under, and the present participle holds the action open beside the aorist ἀπέκτεινεν: the dipping is the killing.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος πρὸς ἄνδρας οἳ τὴν ἀλήθειαν οὐκ εἰδότες ἀπατᾶν νομίζουσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos pros andras hoi tēn alētheian ouk eidotes apatan nomizousin.
sentences.l: The fable is directed at men who, not knowing the truth, think they are deceiving.
sentences.n: νομίζω with a bare infinitive means 'think that one is doing' the thing oneself, the subject of the infinitive being the same as the subject of the verb. εἰδότες is the participle of οἶδα, 'know', which is a perfect with present force.
